title: Drowsy with pinpoint pupils on morphine — prioritise the dangerous decision

blocks.text: Drowsy with pinpoint pupils on morphine — prioritise the dangerous decision

AMaC MRCP PACES23 • Round 5 • R5-231 • Station 2: Consultation (acute presentation) • 20 minutes • Skills A–G (clinical examination as indicated) • 14 October 2026 • Unofficial educational marking descriptors

A 79-year-old receiving morphine for cancer pain has become drowsy. Their eGFR has fallen during an acute illness. The nurse reports slow breathing. Review the patient and explain the immediate plan to a worried relative. Take a focused history, assess immediate safety and agree the initial management with the patient or caller.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: Suspected opioid toxicity due to accumulation of morphine metabolites in renal impairment; other metabolic or intracranial causes remain possible.

TRAP: Never give a large reflex naloxone bolus to a physically dependent palliative patient unless needed for life-threatening compromise: it can precipitate acute pain and withdrawal. Equally, do not let goals-of-care discussions delay rescue of unexpected reversible respiratory depression.

rows: “I need to check whether you need urgent help.”

Never give a large reflex naloxone bolus to a physically dependent palliative patient unless needed for life-threatening compromise: it can precipitate acute pain and withdrawal. Equally, do not let goals-of-care discussions delay rescue of unexpected reversible respiratory depression.
“I’ll ask questions that distinguish the causes.”

Check respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, conscious level, pupils, timing and cumulative opioid doses, recent changes, renal function and co-sedatives. Ask about expressed ceilings of care and current pain control.
“There is a concern that needs checking.”
Suspected opioid toxicity due to accumulation of morphine metabolites in renal impairment; other metabolic or intracranial causes remain possible.
ABCDE, urgent bedside glucose and blood gas as indicated; renal function, medication review and clinical monitoring. Call senior and specialist palliative-care support.

Initiates emergency ABCDE escalation for respiratory depression
Reviews morphine doses, renal function and additional sedatives
Recognises accumulation of active morphine metabolites
Considers infection, metabolic encephalopathy, stroke and other sedatives
Coordinates urgent targeted observations, glucose and blood tests
Continues morphine unchanged despite respiratory depression
Temporarily withholds or reduces opioid and provides appropriate airway/ventilatory support
Seeks specialist palliative input for opioid rotation adjusted for renal failure
Gives a large reflex naloxone bolus regardless of context
If significant opioid-induced respiratory depression occurs, uses carefully titrated naloxone according to emergency and local palliative protocols
Balances restoration of ventilation against acute withdrawal and loss of analgesia; monitors for recurrent toxicity
Tells family all pain medication is permanently stopped
Explains suspected toxicity, monitoring and planned safer analgesia
Checks goals of care and maintains symptom relief while managing risk

blocks.text: Relative says “Are you taking all their pain relief away?” Encourage explanation of comfort-preserving titration. Give only history elicited by candidate; do not volunteer the diagnosis or investigation results.

“The first decision is whether the patient needs emergency assessment now.”

“Before assuming that diagnosis, I should consider: Differentiate medication-related sedation from sepsis, hypercalcaemia, cerebral pathology or other sedatives; a pinpoint pupil alone does not prove opioid toxicity.”

“The specific action I must not omit is: Never give a large reflex naloxone bolus to a physically dependent palliative patient unless needed for life-threatening compromise: it can precipitate acute pain and withdrawal. Equally, do not let goals-of-care discussions delay rescue of unexpected reversible respiratory depression.”

Differential — Considers infection, metabolic encephalopathy, stroke and other sedatives. Coordinates urgent targeted observations, glucose and blood tests
Treatment — Temporarily withholds or reduces opioid and provides appropriate airway/ventilatory support. Seeks specialist palliative input for opioid rotation adjusted for renal failure

THINK: Suspected opioid toxicity due to accumulation of morphine metabolites in renal impairment; other metabolic or intracranial causes remain possible. SAY: explain uncertainty clearly. DO: ABCDE, urgent bedside glucose and blood gas as indicated; renal function, medication review and clinical monitoring. Call senior and specialist palliative-care support. NUMBERS: 20-minute consultation. TRAP: Never give a large reflex naloxone bolus to a physically dependent palliative patient unless needed for life-threatening compromise: it can precipitate acute pain and withdrawal. Equally, do not let goals-of-care discussions delay rescue of unexpected reversible respiratory depression. FINISH: Withhold further opioid temporarily and support airway/breathing. If clinically significant opioid-induced respiratory depression, use cautiously titrated naloxone according to local guidance, aiming to restore ventilation rather than abolish analgesia; repeat/infuse if needed with monitoring. Review opioid choice and dose with palliative specialists for renal failure.
